extracted.intended_audience: public company registrants, auditors/assurance providers, securities lawyers, compliance officers, and policy commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, standards, and stakeholder considerations governing attestation/assurance over registrant GHG emissions disclosures (Scopes 1, 2, and certain Scope 3 metrics), including applicable filing timing, levels of assurance, phase-in schedules, and related implementation concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition-year disclosure for registrants becoming LAF
rubrics_metrics.description: If a registrant becomes a Large Accelerated Filer (LAF) during the fiscal year, it must present required disclosures for the most recently completed fiscal year in which it became an LAF; it is not required to provide those disclosures for prior fiscal years included in its filing when it was not an LAF, to the extent that information was not previously required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to transition-year registrants; they should provide disclosures for the fiscal year in which they attained LAF status but need not retroactively prepare earlier years' disclosures that were not previously required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement for GHG metrics in Form S-3 (225-day rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Form S-3 registration statements, the GHG emissions metrics disclosure incorporated by reference must be as of the registrant's most recently completed fiscal year that is at least 225 days prior to the date of effectiveness of the Form S-3 registration statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the effectiveness date is less than 225 days after its most recently completed fiscal year-end, a registrant will only be required to disclose its GHG emissions for the fiscal year immediately prior to its most recently completed fiscal year if the registrant was required to disclose Scope 1 and/or Scope 2 emissions for that prior year. Similar provision added to Form F-3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form 10-Q/10-K filing timing interaction (225-day calculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Form 10-Q filing deadline for an LAF or AF is within 40 days after the fiscal quarter end (42 days if the 40th day falls on a Saturday), and the end of the second fiscal quarter is 181 days (182 in leap year) after the most recently completed fiscal year — the 225-day deadline accounts for combined upper-limit filing periods (42 + 182 = 224 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This calculation underpins the 225-day effective-date rule for incorporating GHG metrics by reference and establishes how Form 10-Q/10-K filing windows affect required disclosure timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of assurance: limited vs reasonable (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited assurance is equivalent to the assurance level commonly referred to as a 'review' over interim financial statements (negative assurance). Reasonable assurance is equivalent to the level of assurance provided in an audit of consolidated financial statements (positive assurance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited assurance expresses a conclusion about whether the reviewer is aware of any material modifications needed; reasonable assurance expresses an opinion that the subject matter is free from material misstatement in all material respects. The Release cites AICPA SSAE standards (e.g., SSAE No. 22 AT-C section 210 for limited; SSAE No. 21 AT-C sections 205/206 for reasonable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective of limited assurance engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective is for the service provider to express a conclusion in the form of negative assurance about whether it is aware of any material modifications that should be made to the subject matter (e.g., Scopes 1 and 2 disclosures) for it to be fairly stated or in accordance with relevant criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited assurance engagements are analogous to reviews and result in negative assurance language; Release references SSAE No. 22 (AT-C 210) and notes potential limitations (higher probability of overlooking material misstatements compared to reasonable assurance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective of reasonable assurance engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective is to express a positive assurance opinion on whether the subject matter is in accordance with the relevant criteria, in all material respects — i.e., provide an opinion that the subject matter is free from material misstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable assurance involves more extensive examination and testing (including evaluation/testing of internal controls) and is the same level of assurance as a financial statement audit; the Release cites SSAE No. 21 (AT-C 205/206).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary attestation and scope for voluntary submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: An AF or LAF may voluntarily include an attestation report at the limited assurance level for GHG intensity metrics or for Scope 3 disclosures, even where not mandated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission noted examples where registrants voluntarily obtained limited assurance for certain climate metrics and that voluntary assurance options exist within the proposed framework (e.g., voluntary limited assurance for intensity metrics or Scope 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of current market practice on assurance uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys and analyses indicate a substantial portion of large companies already obtain some form of assurance over climate-related metrics, with many of those engagements being limited assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited sources include CAQ and KPMG surveys (e.g., many S&P 500/100 companies obtaining assurance, and within those, a majority obtaining limited assurance). The Commission used staff analysis (March 3, 2022) showing many S&P 500 firms are LAFs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential market confusion from fragmented voluntary assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: International organizations have identified a perceived lack of clarity and consistency around the purpose and scope of voluntary assurance, which can lead to market confusion, misleading investors, and an 'expectations gap.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IOSCO and IFAC reports are cited as highlighting fragmentation as a reason to consider standardized attestation requirements or clearer assurance frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost distribution and mitigation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission stated that for many LAFs already obtaining assurance, incremental compliance costs would be mitigated, and larger issuers generally bear proportionately lower compliance costs than smaller issuers because of fixed cost components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost mitigation expectation is tied to prevalence of voluntary assurance among large issuers; commenters dispute magnitude and distribution of costs, especially for smaller registrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of attestation requirement across registrant size classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders debated whether the attestation requirement should apply to all registrants or be limited (e.g., to AFs and LAFs), with many commenters urging exclusion or delayed application for smaller reporting companies (SRCs) and non-accelerated filers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments include support for applying to all registrants, recommendations for phased-in application by size/filing status, and suggestions for market-based or voluntary approaches instead of mandatory attestation for smaller entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability/capacity of qualified assurance providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters expressed concern that the current supply of qualified assurance providers is insufficient to meet demand, which could trigger a surge in costs and staffing shortages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several law firms and industry groups noted a likely near-term shortage of qualified providers and recommended delaying mandatory attestation until capacity and standards develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-benefit concerns about mandatory attestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters argued that mandatory third-party attestation would impose substantial costs without corresponding investor benefits and proposed alternatives such as self-certification or reliance on existing SEC enforcement and comment processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested alternatives include market-based assurance, disclosure of whether and what type of assurance was obtained, or delaying mandatory requirements until evidence shows net investor benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement challenges and reliance on third-party/estimated data
rubrics_metrics.description: GHG emissions metrics (particularly Scope 1 and Scope 2) can include significant measurement challenges, reliance on third-party data, estimates, and emissions factors that may be difficult to verify under current capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted that much Scope 1/2 data are based on extrapolations or third-party data that may not be amenable to verification today, arguing this complicates reasonable-assurance engagements and supports phased or delayed requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for attestation standards and readiness before mandating higher assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Many commenters requested that the Commission wait to require reasonable assurance until attestation standards, interpretive guidance, and industry readiness have developed and a standards-setting body or clear leadership has emerged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations included deferral until generally accepted climate disclosure attestation principles exist, working with industry participants and standards-setters, and monitoring implementation before shifting from limited to reasonable assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-in schedules and differentiated transition periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended various phased implementation schedules — e.g., longer phase-in for SRCs/smaller registrants, delayed timelines from limited to reasonable assurance, and staggered application by market capitalization or filer type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested timelines ranged from immediate limited assurance with delayed reasonable assurance, multi-year phase-ins (e.g., 2–6 years), or waiting multiple years before any mandatory attestation to allow capacity building and internal system development.

rubrics_metrics.name: International alignment and comparability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters urged attention to alignment with international rules (e.g., EU Regulation) and standards to avoid inconsistencies in scope, timing, and level of assurance that could burden preparers and auditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some requested the SEC assess differences with EU requirements and consider the implications for preparers and auditors' readiness; others recommended harmonizing with ISO or other international assurance frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of specific assurance standards (e.g., ISO 14064-3) for limited assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters (e.g., ANSI NAB) recommended allowing limited assurance engagements to be performed in accordance with ISO 14064-3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recommendation suggests explicit recognition of established international assurance standards as acceptable bases for complying with limited-assurance attestation requirements.
